passage:
Dear Keerthana,

Three months into the job and I wanted to tell you something. My manager wants twenty report summaries a day, made with the AI tool, and I've never once been asked whether I understand them. Speed is all that gets praised.

Last Thursday I found a wrong figure in a summary that had already gone to a client. It was the tool's mistake, but I sent it without checking. My hands went cold. My first thought was to say "the software did it."

Instead I told my manager the same day, showed the correct figure and offered to check the other summaries from that week. The manager just said "okay, fix it". Not warm, but fine.

From now on I check every number myself.

Ayesha

qa.q: How many report summaries a day does the manager want?
qa.a: The manager wants twenty report summaries a day.

qa.q: How did Ayesha feel on finding the wrong figure, and what was the first thought?
qa.a: Ayesha felt panicked: Ayesha's hands went cold, and the first thought was to hide behind the tool by saying "the software did it".

qa.q: What did Ayesha do that was right, and what will change?
qa.a: Ayesha told the manager the same day, showed the correct figure and offered to recheck the week's summaries; from now on Ayesha will check every number personally. 🙂

qa.q: How does the manager seem to see the mistake?
qa.a: The manager said "okay, fix it", not warmly, which suggests the concern is correcting the work quickly, not asking whether Ayesha understands it.

grounding: An employer expects AI-level speed and never asks about understanding, so Ayesha checks accuracy personally and speaks up about the error.

passage:
You know my job, Avni, the market research firm? I thought I'd be learning. I'm Bhupen, by the way, in case your recorder needs a name. My manager gave us the AI tool on day one and said, "Forty summaries a day. Nobody cares how." Nobody asks if I understand the data. They just count.

For two months I pasted, skimmed, sent. Then a client called furious. One of my summaries said their sales in Nagpur went up. They had gone down. The tool had flipped a column.

My manager asked, "Who sent this?" and my first instinct was to say the tool did it. But I sent it.

So I owned it. Then I told the manager I'd found two more errors like that and asked for thirty minutes a day to check numbers. She sighed, but she agreed.

qa.q: How many summaries a day did the manager expect?
qa.a: The manager expected forty summaries a day.

qa.q: What was Bhupen feeling when the manager asked who sent the summary?
qa.a: Bhupen felt tempted to hide behind the tool out of fear, but also a sense of responsibility, because Bhupen had sent it.

qa.q: What did Bhupen do to fix the problem?
qa.a: Bhupen owned the mistake, reported two more errors, and asked for thirty minutes a day to check the numbers.

qa.q: How might the manager see Bhupen's request after the client's complaint?
qa.a: The manager may feel annoyed at the lost speed, but also relieved that someone is checking before another angry client calls.

grounding: The monologue shows a young employee whose manager only counts output, who owns a mistake, checks accuracy and speaks up about errors.

passage:
Monday. Urmila, the team lead at the logistics start-up, dropped a list on Jatin's desk. "Use the AI for route plans. Twenty by noon." She didn't look up from her phone when he asked which data it pulled from.

Thursday. A delivery driver called Jatin, confused. The plan sent him to a warehouse that had closed in January. Jatin checked: the tool had used an old address list. His stomach sank. Three more plans used the same list.

Next Monday. Jatin went to Urmila's desk before she could leave for a meeting. "Four route plans last week had a closed warehouse. I've fixed them. Can we update the address list and let me check plans before they go out?" Urmila frowned, then said, "Put it in writing." He did, that afternoon. By Friday the old list was gone.

qa.q: What had the tool sent the driver to?
qa.a: It sent him to a warehouse that had closed in January.

qa.q: What was Jatin feeling when he found the old address list?
qa.a: Jatin felt a sinking dread, realising more plans were wrong and that no one had been checking.

qa.q: How did Jatin speak up effectively?
qa.a: Jatin gave specific facts, said he had fixed them, proposed updating the list and checking plans, and put it in writing when asked.

qa.q: How might the delivery driver have felt when sent to the closed warehouse?
qa.a: The driver would likely feel confused and frustrated, losing time on a wrong route because of an unchecked plan.

grounding: The three beats show a young employee with an indifferent lead who checks the AI's accuracy himself and speaks up about errors.
